quests.instruction: Oxygen leaves your blood and enters the body's cells through the tiniest blood vessels. What are they called?
quests.hint: They are thinner than a hair.
quests.explanation: Capillary walls are so thin that oxygen and nutrients pass through them, while waste passes back into the blood.
quests.funFact: Red blood cells squeeze through capillaries in single file.

quests.instruction: The windpipe splits into two smaller tubes, one going to each lung. What are they called?
quests.hint: They branch inside the lungs like an upside-down tree.
quests.explanation: The bronchi carry air into each lung, where they divide into smaller and smaller tubes.
quests.funFact: The right bronchus is wider and straighter than the left, so small things that are breathed in tend to go down that side.

quests.instruction: Which tiny cells carry messages along your nerves by sending small electrical signals?
quests.hint: They have long, thin branches that reach out to other cells.
quests.explanation: Nerve cells pass signals from one to the next, like runners in a relay.
quests.funFact: Some nerve cells are more than a meter long, stretching from your lower back to your toes.

quests.instruction: Before your voice can make any sound, something has to push air up past your vocal cords. Which parts supply that air?
quests.hint: Singers train them to hold lots of air.
quests.explanation: Your lungs push air up through the voice box, and the vibrating vocal cords turn it into sound.
quests.funFact: That is why you cannot talk well while holding your breath.

quests.instruction: Before your stomach can digest a sandwich, which parts must first cut and grind it into small pieces?
quests.hint: They work in your mouth.
quests.explanation: Smaller pieces give digestive juices more surface to work on, so chewing starts the job of digestion.
quests.funFact: Chewing slowly also gives your brain time to notice that you are getting full.

quests.instruction: You step into the hot sun, and soon you start to sweat. Which part notices the heat and decides to start sweating, like a thermostat?
quests.hint: It is the control center, not the part that does the sweating.
quests.explanation: Sensors send a warning to the brain, and the brain tells the sweat glands in your skin to release sweat to cool you.
quests.funFact: Your normal body temperature is about 37 degrees Celsius, or 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

quests.instruction: Which soft areas near the ends of a child's long bones make the bones grow longer?
quests.hint: They are the reason you get taller.
quests.explanation: At each growth plate, new bone is added as you grow, so your arms and legs get longer.
quests.funFact: Growth plates harden into solid bone when you finish growing, usually in the teen years.

quests.instruction: Which joint in front of each ear lets your mouth open and close, and slide from side to side as you chew?
quests.hint: You can feel it move if you rest a finger just in front of your ear and open wide.
quests.explanation: The jaw joint works like a hinge that can also slide, which helps you bite and grind food.
quests.funFact: It is one of the most used joints in your body, because you chew, talk, and swallow all day.

quests.instruction: Which small, finger-shaped pouch hangs from the large intestine on the lower right side of your tummy?
quests.hint: It is about as long as your pinky.
quests.explanation: The appendix is a small pouch attached to the large intestine.
quests.funFact: Doctors remove an infected appendix, and people live healthy lives without it.

quests.instruction: Imagine a straight line from your belly button, through your body, and out the other side. Which bone does it run into on the way out?
quests.hint: It runs down your back.
quests.explanation: The spine lies along the back of the trunk, so a line from the front of your tummy reaches it just before leaving your back.
quests.funFact: The soft front of your abdomen and the stiff spine at the back are why you can bend forward easily.

quests.instruction: Which long, flat organ tucked behind your stomach makes juices that help digest food?
quests.hint: It lies right behind the stomach.
quests.explanation: The pancreas sends digestive juices into the small intestine, and it also makes a hormone called insulin.
quests.funFact: The pancreas is about as long as a hand.

quests.instruction: Which small, curved bone at the very bottom of your spine is nicknamed the tailbone?
quests.hint: You sit close to it.
quests.explanation: The tailbone is made of a few small bones joined together at the bottom of the spine.
quests.funFact: It is a leftover from the tail that our very distant ancestors had.

quests.instruction: Which kind of joint lets small bones slide over one another, like the many little bones in your wrist?
quests.hint: Think of two flat surfaces sliding.
quests.explanation: In gliding joints, flat bone surfaces slide a little, and together they let your wrist and ankle flex in many ways.
quests.funFact: Gliding joints also link the bones of your spine.

quests.instruction: Which C-shaped pad of cartilage cushions the inside of your knee joint?
quests.hint: It looks like a little crescent.
quests.explanation: The meniscus acts like a shock absorber between the thigh bone and the shin bone.
quests.funFact: Meniscus comes from a Greek word for crescent moon.

quests.instruction: Between your wrist and your fingers are five long bones that make up the inside of your hand. What are they?
quests.hint: You can feel them under the skin on the back of your hand.
quests.explanation: Palm bones connect the wrist bones to the finger bones and give your hand its shape.
quests.funFact: The proper name for the palm bones is metacarpals.

quests.instruction: Which system uses chemical messengers called hormones, carried in your blood, to help control growth and energy?
quests.hint: Its messengers travel through the blood.
quests.explanation: The endocrine system's glands release hormones that tell different parts of your body what to do.
quests.funFact: Hormones work more slowly than nerve signals, but their effects can last for hours.

quests.instruction: Kidneys, the bladder, and the tubes that connect them work together as which system?
quests.hint: It cleans the blood and gets rid of extra water.
quests.explanation: The urinary system filters waste from the blood and removes it as pee.
quests.funFact: Adults make about one to two liters of pee a day.

quests.instruction: Bones, joints, cartilage, and ligaments together make up which system, the frame of your body?
quests.hint: It gives you shape and protects soft organs.
quests.explanation: The skeletal system holds you up, protects your organs, and gives your muscles something to pull on.
quests.funFact: The skeletal system also stores minerals such as calcium and phosphorus.

quests.instruction: Which chemical messenger, made in the pancreas, helps your cells take sugar out of your blood?
quests.hint: People who cannot make enough of it need to take it as medicine.
quests.explanation: After a meal, sugar enters your blood. Insulin tells your cells to take the sugar in and use it for energy.
quests.funFact: Insulin was first used as a medicine in 1922.

quests.instruction: Which greenish-yellow juice, made by the liver, helps break up fat in your food?
quests.hint: It is stored in a small sac under the liver.
quests.explanation: Bile breaks fat into tiny droplets, which makes it easier for your body to digest.
quests.funFact: Bile is what gives poop its brown color.

quests.instruction: When you feel scared or very excited, your body releases a chemical that makes your heart pound. What is it called?
quests.hint: It gets your body ready for action.
quests.explanation: Adrenaline, made by glands on top of your kidneys, speeds up your heart and breathing so you can react fast.
quests.funFact: The jittery rush you feel before a race or a big performance is adrenaline.

quests.instruction: Which four teeth are usually the last to come in, often in the late teens or early twenties?
quests.hint: They are the last to arrive, far back in the mouth.
quests.explanation: Wisdom teeth are the third set of molars, and they arrive when people are older and, ideally, wiser.
quests.funFact: Many people do not have enough room in their jaws for wisdom teeth.

quests.instruction: By about age five, which part of your body has already grown to nearly its full adult size?
quests.hint: It grows fastest in early childhood.
quests.explanation: A child's brain grows very quickly in the first years of life, reaching about 90 percent of its adult size by age five.
quests.funFact: Playing, talking, and reading with young children help build connections between their nerve cells.

quests.instruction: Which small, pear-shaped sac tucked under the liver stores bile until the body needs it?
quests.hint: It holds a greenish juice.
quests.explanation: The gallbladder squirts stored bile into the small intestine after a meal that contains fat.
quests.funFact: A person can live a normal life without a gallbladder.

quests.instruction: Sound enters your ear, the cochlea turns it into signals, and a nerve carries them to your brain. What is that nerve called?
quests.hint: It does for the ear what the optic nerve does for the eye.
quests.explanation: The hearing nerve carries signals from the cochlea to the brain, which turns them into sounds you recognize.
quests.funFact: A hearing nerve has about thirty thousand nerve fibers.

quests.instruction: The tiniest branches of your lungs end in clusters of microscopic air sacs, where oxygen passes into your blood. What are the air sacs called?
quests.hint: They look like tiny bunches of grapes.
quests.explanation: Alveoli have very thin walls, so oxygen can slip into the blood and carbon dioxide can slip out.
quests.funFact: Your two lungs hold about 480 million alveoli.

quests.instruction: Sunshine falling on which part of you helps your body make vitamin D?
quests.hint: It is the part that tans or burns in the sun.
quests.explanation: Sunlight on your skin helps your body make vitamin D, which helps you take in the calcium that bones need.
quests.funFact: Fish, eggs, and fortified milk also give you vitamin D.

quests.instruction: Think of the organs in your trunk as floors in a building, from your chest down to your pelvis. Which one is on the lowest floor?
quests.hint: It sits in the pelvis.
quests.explanation: The lungs are in the chest, the stomach is in the upper abdomen, and the bladder is low in the pelvis.
quests.funFact: As the bladder fills, its wall stretches like a balloon.

quests.instruction: Beneath a tooth's hard outer enamel is a layer that makes up most of the tooth. What is it called?
quests.hint: It is about as hard as bone.
quests.explanation: Dentin sits between the enamel and the pulp and gives the tooth its strength and shape.
quests.funFact: Dentin is slightly yellow, which is why teeth can look yellower when the enamel wears thin.

quests.instruction: Fresh, oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs to the heart. Which side of the heart then pumps it out to the rest of the body?
quests.hint: It is the stronger side, with thicker walls.
quests.explanation: The left side receives blood from the lungs and pumps it out to the body, while the right side sends used blood to the lungs.
quests.funFact: The left side's thick muscle walls help it push blood much farther than the right side does.
